claims.text: The equiatomic quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy has a higher prevalence of short-range chemical ordering than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater lattice distortion and short-range chemical ordering increase dislocation pinning.
Greater lattice distortion and short-range chemical ordering alter slip-system activity relative to the reduced-component alloys.
The proposed dislocation-pinning mechanism enhances yield strength and work hardening in the quinary alloy.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary equiatomic alloys are thermomechanically processed and single-phase FCC.
Removing one or two constituents from the quinary alloy diminishes local lattice-distortion and chemical-ordering effects.
Differences in atomic size and bonding in the quinary alloy generate non-uniform local stresses.
Differences in atomic size and bonding in the quinary alloy promote solute clustering.
Non-uniform local stresses and solute clustering increase dislocation pinning.
Under identical room-temperature, constant-strain-rate testing, the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy will have higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Under identical room-temperature, constant-strain-rate testing, the quinary alloy will have a steeper work-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys will maintain similar levels of ductility.
The proposed comparison is applicable only when the alloys remain single-phase FCC, receive identical thermomechanical processing, and are tested at room temperature under the same strain rate.
Differences in processing can influence the extent of short-range chemical order.
